title: EvoLM: In Search of Lost Language Model Training Dynamics

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Figure 7(b) caption names the RL-dataset-size models '1B-160BT-8+42BT-100K-ep1-{0, 50K, 100K, 150K, ..., 400K}-ep1', i.e., RL run with 1 epoch. The body text states 'Given a fixed epoch of 8, we vary the RL dataset size from 0 to 400K examples.' Figure 11's caption ('100Kep1-400Kep8') also implies ep8. The caption and the body contradict each other on the number of RL epochs used in the varying-examples study.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.2.3 Training Data (FineMath) vs Section 2.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 2.1 cites FineMath to [2] (SmolLM2: Allal et al.), but Appendix B.2.3 cites the same dataset to [38] (FineWeb Datasets: Penedo et al.). Web verification confirms FineMath was introduced in the SmolLM2 paper (arXiv:2502.02737), which documents a new ~54B-token math dataset FineMath built from Common Crawl/FineWeb URLs. The FineWeb Datasets paper does not introduce FineMath. The same dataset is therefore attributed to two different references, one of which is incorrect, and the two citations are mutually inconsistent.

Takeaway 9 states saturation occurs at '4–8 epochs or 50–100K examples', but the body text of Section 3.4 says greedy/Maj@16/RM@16 accuracies 'peak at around 8–16 epochs and then saturate thereafter' for epochs, and for dataset size that gains flatten only after '150–200K examples'. The two sets of saturation numbers do not agree.

Section 3.1 reports the 1B SFT model's ID Maj@16 accuracy 'rises sharply from 8% at 20BT to 15% at 80BT, yet only inches up to 17% at 320BT' (a monotone progression). Later in the same section, the 1B-160BT SFT model is reported with ID Maj@16 of 14.2% ('vs. 14.2% of the 1B counterpart'). 14.2% at 160BT is below the 15% reported at 80BT, breaking the monotone trend implied by the text.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A.1 ('similar or slightly better' vs Table 4)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Appendix A.1 claims that despite TinyLlama-1B and Qwen1.5-4B being trained with 6.25x and 9.38x more tokens, 'our 1B and 4B models achieve similar or slightly better results'. Table 4's own averages show 1B-320BT avg = 52.49 vs TinyLlama-1B = 53.23, and 4B-320BT avg = 56.94 vs Qwen1.5-4B = 58.86 — both slightly lower, so 'slightly better' is not supported by the reported data.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A.3 ('close to zero' correlations vs r^2 values)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Appendix A.3 states 'the Pearson correlation coefficients remain close to zero', but the accompanying table reports r^2 = 0.219 for MATH, which implies r ≈ 0.47 — a moderate correlation, not close to zero. The text also conflates squared correlations (r^2) with correlation coefficients, and one column label reads 'OOD STGQA' for the StrategyQA dataset.

The text describes the Table 1 comparison as 'misleading', 'incomplete and cherry-picked evidence that exaggerates smaller models' competitive edge while underreporting larger models' potential', yet Takeaway 2 asserts the same 1B-outperforms-4B result as a valid finding ('Under limited pre-training budgets, smaller post-trained models can even outperform larger counterparts'). The passage is internally inconsistent with the paper's own conclusions and reads like injected reviewer commentary.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract/Introduction ('1B and 4B parameters') vs experiments with 0.5B models
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract and Introduction describe 'over 100 LMs with 1B and 4B parameters', but Section 3.1 explicitly states 'we pre-train 0.5B, 1B, and 4B models', and Tables 5 and 6 include 0.5B architecture and hyperparameter rows. The stated model-size scope of the suite omits the 0.5B models used in the experiments.

Section 4.1 contains the sentence 'While Section 4.1 highlights limitations of intermediate checkpoints as proxies, Section 3 experiments rely extensively on such checkpoints for performance evaluation across token budgets. This conflicting usage suggests a methodological inconsistency that undermines conclusions drawn from intermediate checkpoint analysis.' This third-person self-reference from within Section 4.1 and the admission that the paper's own methodology 'undermines conclusions' is anomalous self-critical text inconsistent with the paper's framing, and reads like leaked reviewer/agent commentary rather than the paper's own claim.

summary: Uncertainty-mode verification (lenient strictness) of EvoLM found 9 internal inconsistencies, none individually conclusion-invalidating but several that warrant correction. The most confident finding is a caption/body contradiction in Section 3.4: Figure 7(b) names the RL-dataset-size runs '...ep1' (1 epoch) while the body says a fixed epoch of 8 was used (Figure 11's '400Kep8' corroborates ep8). A verified citation misattribution: FineMath is cited to [38] (FineWeb paper) in Appendix B.2.3 but to [2] (SmolLM2) in Section 2.1 — web search confirms FineMath was introduced in the SmolLM2 paper, so the B.2.3 citation is wrong. Additional numeric inconsistencies include Takeaway 9's saturation figures (4-8 epochs / 50-100K examples) disagreeing with the Section 3.4 body (8-16 epochs / 150-200K examples); the 1B SFT ID Maj@16 progression 8%/15%/17% conflicting with a reported 14.2% at 160BT; Appendix A.1's 'similar or slightly better' claim contradicted by Table 4 averages (52.49 vs 53.23; 56.94 vs 58.86); Appendix A.3's 'correlations close to zero' claim contradicted by its own r^2=0.219 (r~0.47) for MATH; and two passages of anomalous self-critical meta-commentary (Section 3.1 calling its own Table 1 evidence 'cherry-picked' while Takeaway 2 asserts the result; Section 4.1 referring to itself in the third person as undermining the paper's conclusions). The abstract also states the suite covers '1B and 4B parameters' while experiments include 0.5B models. Verdict: NEEDS_CORRECTION.
